prompt: What is the engineer's particular trap in a conversation about a need, by the lesson?
hint: What starts at the first noun?

choices.text: Solving from the first noun and hearing nothing after it
choices.why: Right: Lívia had an estimate ten seconds after "recommendations".

choices.text: Talking too little, so the other person feels ignored
choices.why: Silence is a separate failure; the trap is about where attention goes.

choices.text: Agreeing too quickly to every request that comes from product
choices.why: The trap is solving, not agreeing.

choices.text: Using too much jargon
choices.why: Lesson 3's problem, not this one.

prompt: Match each row of the table to how it differs when listening to understand.

pairs.right: what they are saying and why
the problem they are trying to describe
room for them to go on
a question, or a summary to check

prompt: Which of these is active listening, by the lesson?
hint: Three are on the "is not" list.

choices.text: Agreeing with the solution so the speaker feels heard
choices.why: Understanding commits you to nothing about the solution.

choices.text: Staying silent until the speaker has finished everything
choices.why: Silence gives no evidence of being understood.

choices.text: Showing the speaker what you understood
choices.why: Right: hearing the whole meaning and showing that you heard it.

choices.text: Nodding and repeating the last three words at intervals
choices.why: Noticed within a minute, and worse than inattention.

prompt: Which is a paraphrase in the lesson's sense?
hint: Your words, short, with a real question.

choices.text: "So you need a recommendations service."
choices.why: Repeating proves only that you can repeat.

choices.text: "OK, I will scope a recommendations service by Friday."
choices.why: That is a commitment to the solution, not a check.

choices.text: "Let me tell you how we would build that, then you tell me if it fits."
choices.why: A speech of your own, about the solution.

choices.text: "You want returning customers to buy more. Is that it?"
choices.why: Right: the purpose in your words, ending with a question.

prompt: What did Renata's correction to Lívia's paraphrase reveal?

choices.text: The fall had already reversed by April
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson says so.

choices.text: The fall was in returning customers only
choices.why: Right: which pointed at something that changed for people who already used the app.

choices.text: New customers were the real problem all along
choices.why: The opposite: new customers were fine.

choices.text: Leadership had already approved a recommendations service
choices.why: Leadership wanted an explanation, not a specific project.

prompt: Renata says "everybody upstairs is asking me why". Which response does the lesson recommend?
hint: About her situation, not about her.

choices.text: "Don't worry, we'll build it fast."
choices.why: A promise about a solution nobody has understood yet.

choices.text: "It sounds like you need something to tell the board by the review."
choices.why: Right: an observation about her situation that she can confirm or correct.

choices.text: Ignore it, since it is not a requirement
choices.why: It was the most important sentence she said.

choices.text: "You seem stressed about this."
choices.why: A statement about her, which most people at work resent.

prompt: Why does the lesson warn against asking "Is the problem the home screen?" early on?
hint: Whose guess ends up in the answer?

choices.text: Because it is rude to suggest a cause
choices.why: Politeness is not the issue.

choices.text: Because closed questions are banned in discovery conversations
choices.why: They are for the end, to confirm facts.

choices.text: Because the home screen was not in fact the cause
choices.why: It turned out to be close to the cause, and the warning holds anyway.

choices.text: It imports the asker's guess into the answer
choices.why: Right: she will think about the home screen whether or not it is the problem.

prompt: What does the lesson suggest asking instead of "Why do you want a recommendations service?"

choices.text: "Who asked you for it?"
choices.why: That sounds more like a challenge, not less.

choices.text: "What would it change?"
choices.why: Right: it asks for the purpose without asking her to justify herself.

choices.text: Nothing; just start scoping
choices.why: That is the trap from the first section.

choices.text: "Are you sure that is what you need, given what it would cost the teams?"
choices.why: A closed question carrying a judgement.

prompt: Put Lívia's questions in the order of the funnel.
items: What changed for returning customers since January?
What do people do on the home screen now?
Is it the returning customers only?

prompt: After a question, the lesson suggests counting silently to how many before speaking?
hint: It feels long and looks thoughtful.

prompt: The returning-customer basket fell from R$ 150 to R$ 138. By what percentage did it fall?
What did the data show about the "buy again" list?

choices.text: New customers had never seen it and were confused by the menu
choices.why: New customers' baskets did not change.

choices.text: It had been removed from the app entirely
choices.why: It moved into a menu; it still existed.

choices.text: Users of it bought as before; fewer opened it
choices.why: Right: so the fix was where it sat, not what it did.

choices.text: Customers who opened it bought less than before
choices.why: They bought as much as before.

prompt: How many days did it take Bruna's team to put the list back on the home screen?
hint: Against a quarter for two teams.

prompt: Suppose returning customers were opening the list as often as ever and still buying less. What follows, by the lesson?

choices.text: The home screen should be redesigned again
choices.why: The list already works in this scenario; the cause is elsewhere.

choices.text: Recommendations become a real candidate, with the R$ 150 measure
choices.why: Right: listening finds out whether the requested solution fits.

choices.text: Nothing can be concluded without a quarter of research
choices.why: The data rules out the cheap fix; it does not freeze the decision.

choices.text: The request should still be refused, since requests are solutions in disguise
choices.why: The lesson says sometimes the person has done the diagnosis.

prompt: Christensen's idea that customers "hire" a product for a task in their lives is called jobs to be ___.
Which parts belong in the written summary after a conversation about a need? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: A full transcript, so nothing is lost
choices.why: A transcript fixes nothing; a summary both sides agreed to does.

choices.text: A request to correct anything wrong by a date
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: The need, separated from the solution first requested
choices.why: Yes.

choices.text: Open questions, each with who will answer it
choices.why: Yes.

prompt: If the basket does not recover, how does Lívia's note help her?
hint: What did it say about recommendations?

choices.text: It proves the data team was wrong
choices.why: The note blames nobody.

choices.text: It lets her say Renata approved the cheaper fix in writing and owns the outcome
choices.why: The note is not a shield against Renata; it records a shared plan.

choices.text: It shows recommendations were left open, with a date
choices.why: Right: kept open on purpose, decided on 12 May with the numbers.

choices.text: It does not; notes are only for memory
choices.why: The lesson names this as one of the reasons it matters.

prompt: "The person who writes the summary decides what the meeting agreed." What does the lesson draw from that?

choices.text: Let the most senior person write it
choices.why: Seniority is not the point.

choices.text: Always volunteer to write it, to steer outcomes
choices.why: That reads it as a privilege, which the lesson rejects.

choices.text: Write what was agreed, send it that day, and ask for corrections
choices.why: Right: not what the writer wished had been agreed.

choices.text: Do not write summaries, to avoid bias
choices.why: Then each person keeps their own drifting version.

prompt: Henrique asks Lívia: "Can you help us pick a message broker?" Following this lesson, what is her best first reply?
hint: The request may be a solution.

choices.text: "Sure. What happens today that a broker would change?"
choices.why: Right: an open question about the situation, before any solution.

choices.text: "Is the problem that your queue is too slow?"
choices.why: A closed question that imports her guess.

choices.text: "Sure, Kafka is the standard choice."
choices.why: Solving at the first noun.

choices.text: "Why do you think you need one at all?"
choices.why: Likely heard as a challenge.
